function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits.

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 32 – Blackout Conditions
     2|
     3|*Mission AI: "Station Day 473, 09:41. I am alerting all personnel to a solar particle event in progress. Solar Observatory at Lagrange Point Two reported an X-class flare six minutes and forty-two seconds after it occurred. The flare originated from Active Region 3847, a sunspot group that has been building magnetic complexity for eleven days. The associated coronal mass ejection reached Earth orbit approximately twenty-two hours later, and I extrapolated its transit velocity to Mars using a modified ballistic propagation model. The solar proton flux at Mars is expected to exceed safe EVA thresholds within forty-one minutes. The total dose rate during the peak of the event could reach thirty to fifty millisieverts per hour at the surface. The event duration, based on comparable historical events, is estimated at thirty-six to sixty hours. During that time, all exterior operations must cease immediately. All personnel must relocate to the deepest available shelter — which is the regolith-buried section of the base along the water storage corridor. This is the second solar event of this magnitude since landing. The first lasted eight hours. This one will be longer. The refugees from Ares Beta have not yet arrived, which means the population is still thirty. For now, the only math that matters is radiation dose, shielding depth, and power reserves."*
     4|
     5|*Arun Das: "Copy the alert. I'm moving to engineering."*
     6|
     7|*Elena Varga: "Mission AI, broadcast the shelter order. All non-essential exterior equipment — secure or abandon and document."*
     8|
     9|*Mission AI: "Broadcasting now."*
    10|
    11|---
    12|
    13|The alert came through the habitat's public address system as a tone Elena had heard only once before — on day 141, when the first solar event forced thirty frightened people into the water corridor and they waited together in the dark, counting the ticks on the dosimeters, wondering if Mars would kill them with invisible fire.
    14|
    15|This time she woke already knowing what was coming. The first solar event had been a surprise. This one carried the weight of forewarning — a satellite had seen the flare, extrapolated a transit, and built a model that said: get underground, get under dirt, get under water, get down, now.
    16|
    17|She was in the corridor in forty seconds, boots unlaced, pulling them on while she moved. The blue emergency lights were already cycling — steady blue, not the pulsing blue of communications but the flat blue of shelter-in-place.
    18|
    19|Gabriel met her at the junction, recorder already running.
    20|
    21|"X-class flare," he said. "CME is inbound. Mission AI estimates peak proton flux in forty to fifty minutes. Duration — thirty-six to sixty hours."
    22|
    23|"Get everyone to the shelter corridor. Laila already has the medical kits. I want a head count within fifteen minutes. If someone is on EVA, Mission AI?"
    24|
    25|*"Imani is already cycling the airlock. She has approximately four minutes before suit decontamination is complete. She will reach the shelter corridor with time to spare."*
    26|
    27|"Tomas?"
    28|
    29|*"Underground since 08:00 local — he was in the machine shop when the alert came. No EVA personnel currently outside the habitat. All confirmed."*
    30|
    31|Elena felt the tightness in her chest ease by a fraction. The first lesson of emergencies on Mars was always the same: count your people before you worry about anything else.
    32|
    33|---
    34|
    35|The shelter corridor ran along the west side of the buried section of the base. One point two meters of Martian dirt overhead, reinforced with load-bearing arches that Jonah had fabricated from salvaged structural steel. The walls were lined with water tanks — twenty-four modular containers, each holding approximately four hundred liters. Water was an excellent radiation shield: hydrogen atoms stopping high-energy protons through momentum transfer between particles of equal mass. The tanks doubled as the colony's water reserve and its best protection against solar radiation. Today both functions needed to be perfect.
    36|
    37|Elena found Laila already in the corridor, medical kits arranged on a folding table stored for exactly this scenario. Two radiation dosimeters sat at either end of the corridor, their digital displays reading the current dose rate in real time. At the moment, the numbers were still low. 3.8 µSv/h. Normal background for the buried habitat.
    38|
    39|"How much time?" Laila asked.
    40|
    41|"Thirty to forty minutes before things change."
    42|
    43|Laila nodded and began organizing supplies with the methodical precision of someone who had done this before. "Forty-eight hours in shelter is the minimum plan. Mission AI's estimate is thirty-six to sixty. I'm packing for the worst case. Psychological effects will be the harder problem. Forty-eight hours of confinement. No windows. Minimal lighting. Three people sleeping in the space normally occupied by one. Put them in a hole under two meters of dirt with no sky and the dose rate climbing and I guarantee someone will need medication by hour twenty."
    44|
    45|"Who?"
    46|
    47|"Ravi for certain — claustrophobic tendencies, manageable in normal conditions, unpredictable under stress. Priya, because she has been managing the greenhouse around the clock and the idea of leaving her plants unsupervised for two days will gnaw at her. And Arun. Not claustrophobia — he will think he needs to be in the machine shop monitoring the reactor, and being down here with no screens will feel like abandonment."
    48|
    49|People were arriving now. Ravi, carrying a small toolkit because that was how he felt useful. Priya, coming straight from the greenhouse, hands empty, face tight. Jonah with a heavy fabrication case, irritated — the man who solved problems by building solutions, and this was a problem no tool could touch. Imani with Tomas, still carrying the physical markers of interrupted work.
    50|
    51|By the time Mission AI confirmed all thirty personnel were accounted for, the dosimeter at the north end of the corridor had begun to rise.
    52|
    53|4.2. 6.1. 12.3. 28.7. 65.4.
    54|
    55|The proton front had arrived.
    56|
    57|"The north dosimeter just crossed sixty microsieverts per hour," Laila said. "Fifteen times increase over normal. The event has begun."
    58|
    59|10:23 local. The storm had started. They waited.
    60|
    61|---
    62|
    63|## Scene 2
    64|
    65|The first hour was routine. Not comfortable but routine — the kind of activity an organization performs well because it has rehearsed it and learned from the prior occurrence. Thirty people settled into the shelter corridor, dimly lit with emergency LEDs at minimum brightness, the water tanks along the walls casting a faint blue wash.
    66|
    67|Arun set up a workstation in the corner — a folding table, a tablet connected to the internal network, a second screen mounted on a water tank. The power management dashboard showed battery charge at ninety-two percent, reactor output at full rating, solar input at zero because the panels were exposed and the proton flux made any surface operation impossible. The Sterling generator was running on waste heat from the reactor, producing approximately twelve kilowatts. Total colony consumption: forty-five kilowatts.
    68|
    69|"Current burn," Arun said to Elena, who stood beside him reading the dashboard the way a commander reads a tactical map. "At forty-five kilowatts and battery reserves of eight hundred kilowatt-hours, we have seventeen hours of autonomy on battery alone. Reactor is running, Sterling is producing twelve kilowatts, so net draw from battery is thirty-three kilowatts. Eight hundred divided by thirty-three — "
    70|
    71|"Approximately twenty-four hours."
    72|
    73|"Twenty-four point two. But if the storm lasts longer than the solar panel exposure window — which it will, based on the initial flux profile — we need to reduce consumption."
    74|
    75|"How much?"
    76|
    77|Arun pulled up a spreadsheet. Four columns: system, power consumption, criticality, recommended reduction. He studied it with the expression of a man running calculations he did not want to run.
    78|
    79|"We need to cut at least forty percent. That means we go from forty-five kilowatts to approximately twenty-seven. Twenty-seven minus the Sterling's twelve — fifteen kilowatts from battery. Eight hundred divided by fifteen: fifty-three hours. That gets us through forty-eight with margin. Anything less and we're gambling on an optimistic event duration."
    80|
    81|"Forty percent cut. What goes."
    82|
    83|"Greenhouse grow lights are the largest consumer after life support — eight kilowatts. Cut to emergency red backup only: one point two. External heaters and airlock de-icing: three kilowatts. Water reclamation auxiliary pumps: two kilowatts. Non-essential interior lighting: one kilowatt. Workshop tools: one and a half. Comfort load — " he paused " — three kilowatts. Climate control in sleeping quarters. Kitchen heating beyond one communal unit. Rec room circulation."
    84|
    85|"The comfort load is the difference between tolerable and miserable."
    86|
    87|"Miserable is survivable. If we burn through battery reserves — "
    88|
    89|"Cut it all," Elena said. "Greenhouse to emergency backup. Airlock heaters off. Workshop off. Kitchen to one heating unit. Climate control to minimum. Everything that keeps people alive stays on. Everything that makes them comfortable is off. Implement it."
    90|
    91|Arun was already typing. "Implementing."
    92|
    93|The corridor lights dropped to near-darkness. The ambient hum of ventilation slowed. Somewhere down the corridor, someone made a small sound that Elena recognized as suppressed frustration.
    94|
    95|Priya stood up. "Arun — the greenhouse. How low did you set the lights?"
    96|
    97|"Emergency red backup. One point two kilowatts total across all racks."
    98|
    99|Priya's face tightened. "The red spectrum isn't sufficient for the current crop. Leafy greens will stop growing within twenty-four hours. The legumes will suffer from lack of blue wavelengths. How much yield will I lose?"
   100|
   101|"Fifteen to twenty percent for forty-eight hours. Twenty to thirty for sixty."
   102|
   103|"Thirty percent." Priya's eyes were doing the arithmetic — calories already budgeted, meals already planned, margins already thin. "That's — "
   104|
   105|"Significant. I know. But a dead greenhouse is worse than a weakened greenhouse."
   106|
   107|Priya stared at him for a long moment, then nodded. Not agreement. Acceptance. The distinction mattered.
   108|
   109|Around her, the colony was settling into the shape of the next forty-eight hours — or sixty — or whatever number the sun decided to give them.
   110|
   111|---
   112|
   113|## Scene 3
   114|
   115|Twelve hours into the event, the corridor felt smaller.
   116|
   117|The walls had not moved — four meters wide, eighteen meters long, one point two meters of regolith overhead, water tanks on both sides, thirty people distributed along the narrow space. But the perception of enclosure deepened with every hour that the dosimeters told them the world outside was hostile.
   118|
   119|Laila moved through the corridor on her second wellness check, dosimeter in one hand, medical tablet in the other, watching people with the specific attention of a physician assessing a population under sustained stress.
   120|
   121|The first twelve hours had been manageable. People talked quietly. Some slept on thin emergency mattresses. A few played a word game Gabriel had invented over the months. But the second twelve hours were different. The signs were appearing.
   122|
   123|Ravi had paced from the north end to the south end and back twice in the last hour. His breathing was fast and shallow — not panicked, not yet, but the kind of accelerated respiration that preceded panic. He kept touching the water tank beside him, feeling the solid plastic, the cool surface, the reassurance of mass.
   124|
   125|"Ravi," Laila said, sitting down.
   126|
   127|He looked at her with the careful intensity of someone concentrating very hard on appearing normal. "I'm fine."
   128|
   129|"Your heart rate is elevated. Your breathing is shallow. Your skin temperature is up one degree Celsius. You are not fine."
   130|
   131|He exhaled, and the exhale was the sound of a dam releasing water in controlled amounts. "I'm managing."
   132|
   133|"With what technique?"
   134|
   135|"Counting. In. Out. Four count in. Four hold. Six count out. The pattern helps when I can control one variable in an environment where I cannot control anything."
   136|
   137|"Good technique. Are you maintaining it?"
   138|
   139|"I was. Until I started thinking about the dosimeter." He gestured toward the display at the north end. 412 µSv/h — forty times the normal buried-habitat rate. "I keep doing the conversion. Four-twelve microsieverts. Zero point four one millisieverts per hour. In twenty-four hours — "
   140|
   141|"Ravi. You are inside a corridor buried under one point two meters of regolith with water tanks on both sides. The dose you are accumulating is approximately fifteen percent of the surface dose. The number on that dosimeter is at the surface, not here. Mission AI has been tracking since the event began. You have accumulated approximately zero point two millisieverts in twelve hours. The equivalent of a cross-country flight."
   142|
   143|Ravi looked at her. "Show me the math?"
   144|
   145|"I will. But I also want you to tell me what you are really counting."
   146|
   147|He was quiet. The ventilation hummed.
   148|
   149|"I'm counting the difference between being here and being outside," Ravi said finally. "Forty-eight hours and I'd still be out there if the alert hadn't come."
   150|
   151|"And now you're not. You're inside under dirt and water. And all of this was designed so that this exact scenario would be survivable." She paused. "It is working."
   152|
   153|Ravi put his head in his hands and breathed. Laila sat with him until his breathing slowed, until the four-count pattern returned to its rhythm. Then she moved to the next person.
   154|
   155|Priya was against the far water tank, knees drawn up, staring at nothing.
   156|
   157|"I keep thinking about the plants," Priya said before Laila could speak. "In the dark. The red lights aren't enough. They're stressed and I can feel it."
   158|
   159|"I know."
   160|
   161|"They're not just the food supply. After everything — the mold, the crop loss, the failed cycles — every green thing in that greenhouse is a vote of confidence. Every leaf is a choice we made to stay on this planet. And right now I've put them in the dark because the sun is trying to kill us and the math said plants had to wait for people." Her voice cracked. "Which is true. It's true. They're in the dark."
   162|
   163|"Priya. They've survived worse. The mold cycle. Nutrient contamination. They survived because they are alive, and alive things want to be alive. You'll lose biomass. Leaves will yellow. But they will survive because you built them a system that makes survival possible. Two days from now you'll go back and you'll find them still growing."
   164|
   165|Priya wiped her face, nodded once.
   166|
   167|---
   168|
   169|Twenty-four hours. The north dosimeter had peaked at 547 µSv/h at approximately hour eighteen and had begun a slow decline — the falling edge of the proton curve, the sun exhausting its ejection of charged particles. But the event was not over, and the corridor was fraying.
   170|
   171|Jonah had been quiet the entire duration, sitting against a water tank with a small flashlight — an indulgence of comfort lighting in a space designed to conserve power — and working on something small in his hands. Laila recognized the pattern: the man who normally solved problems with fabrication was now solving helplessness by making something.
   172|
   173|"What are you building?"
   174|
   175|"A bracket. For the new CO2 scrubber array." He held it up — clean edges, symmetrical geometry, the tactile satisfaction of a thing made correctly. "Arun says we need it ready when the refugees arrive. I figured I might as well be useful."
   176|
   177|"You are being useful by being here, Jonah."
   178|
   179|He set the flashlight down. "Laila. I want to ask you something that isn't a medical question."
   180|
   181|"Ask."
   182|
   183|"When the refugees get here — when sixty people walk through our airlock — will we have room? Not physically. I mean — will we have room." He gestured at the narrow corridor, the water tanks, the crowded bodies, the dim light. "We're thirty. We're already stepping over each other in a space this size. Sixty more people in this hole — we won't have enough floor space to lie down."
   184|
   185|Laila sat beside him. "Jonah. This is a question you're asking because of what you're feeling right now."
   186|
   187|"Maybe. But it's still real."
   188|
   189|"It is. And the answer is: we'll make room. Humans compress when conditions demand it. We did it in submarines, in bunkers, in lifeboats. But you're right to worry — because the worry isn't really about the refugees. It's about whether this colony is still the colony it was before the signal from Ares Beta."
   190|
   191|Jonah was quiet. He put the small bracket in his pocket and picked up the flashlight. "I'm going to make another bracket."
   192|
   193|Laila let him. Fabrication was his coping mechanism, and denying it would be worse than the space problem.
   194|
   195|---
   196|
   197|At hour thirty, the dosimeters began to drop more rapidly — the steep decline of the event's tail. Mission AI estimated the event would end within twelve to fifteen hours. Approximately forty-five hours of total confinement.
   198|
   199|Something shifted. The dosimeters were falling, the worst was passing, but the psychological toll was concentrated. A two-person argument had erupted over temperature — one too warm, one too cold, both correct, neither able to adjust because climate control had been cut to minimum. The slowed ventilation made the air feel thick, and the sensation of breathing heavy air had cascaded into anxiety for several crew members. Ravi had been given a mild anxiolytic. Priya was sleeping fitfully. Imani had been doing push-ups in a corner for forty minutes, burning off restless energy her body demanded but the environment would not permit.
   200|
   201|Elena stood and walked to the center of the corridor.
   202|
   203|"Listen."
   204|
   205|The corridor quieted.
   206|
   207|"The event is winding down. Mission AI estimates we're approximately twelve to fifteen hours from returning to the main habitat. The last thirty hours have been difficult. The air feels heavy. The light is too dim. The space is too small. I can feel it too. I'm not going to pretend it hasn't been hard." She paused. "But I want you to notice something. Notice that the shelter is working. The regolith overhead is stopping most of the radiation. The water tanks are stopping the rest. The dosimeters tell us the surface dose is high and our dose is low, and that's not an accident. That's because on day one hundred and eighty, when Laila told us the math, we chose to bury this base. We chose to move tons of dirt and build arches and install water tanks along the walls. We chose to be uncomfortable during construction so we could be safe during an event like this. Now the event is here, and we are safe."
   208|
   209|She looked around the corridor. Thirty faces in the dim light.
   210|
   211|"The choice we made months ago is protecting us now."
   212|
   213|She sat back down. Someone started crying quietly, and no one asked who it was, and no one needed to, because on Mars, crying in a shelter under dirt was not weakness. It was proof you were still human.
   214|
   215|---
   216|
   217|## Scene 4
   218|
   219|Arun had not left his corner since the event began. He was cycling through screens the way a pilot checks instruments — rhythmically, systematically, returning to each display at regular intervals.
   220|
   221|Power dashboard. Battery reserves. Reactor temperature. Sterling generator output. Atmospheric CO2 — elevated from reduced ventilation but well below dangerous levels. Oxygen production — steady, the scaled-up plant at reduced capacity, sufficient for thirty.
   222|
   223|And the battery charge, which was the number he watched most closely.
   224|
   225|Hour 0: 92%. Hour 12: 81%. Hour 24: 71%. Hour 30: 67%.
   226|
   227|"Mission AI, update the battery discharge projection. Use current flux decline rate and extrapolate event end time."
   228|
   229|*"Processing. Updated projection: event end at approximately Station Day 473, 22:00 — roughly twelve hours from now. Total event duration: approximately forty hours. Battery at current load during remaining event: will discharge to approximately sixty-one percent. After event ends, solar panel output will resume at approximately three kilowatts within the first hour of exposure as panels clear residual dust. Full output will require cleaning — approximately four hours of EVA once the surface dose permits safe egress."*
   230|
   231|Arun did the arithmetic. Sixty-one percent at end of event, plus four hours of minimal solar output, plus reduced load. They'd come out at approximately fifty-five to fifty-seven percent. Comfortably above his forty percent safety line. Survivable.
   232|
   233|The refugee timeline was the variable that kept him awake. The Ares Beta ship was coming. When it arrived, population would go from thirty to approximately ninety-three. Every system — oxygen, water, food — was designed for thirty and already operating at the upper limit during refugee preparation.
   234|
   235|He opened a new calculation.
   236|
   237|Pre-arrival power plan, population 93:
   238|Reactor plus Sterling: 16 kilowatts total
   239|Oxygen plant at 95 percent: 7 kilowatts — critical, no reduction possible
   240|CO2 scrubbers at 90 percent: 4 kilowatts — critical
   241|Water reclamation: 2 kilowatts
   242|Greenhouse emergency backup: 1.2 kilowatts
   243|HVAC minimum: 3 kilowatts

     3|*Mission AI: "Station Day 487, 05:00. In one hour and forty-seven minutes, the colony will vote on a document that has been in development for forty-one days. Forty-one days of draft, redraft, debate, compromise, and synthesis. The document is twelve articles. It is four hundred and sixty-two words. It is the most heavily contested text in human history on the surface of Mars — contested not by armies or governments but by thirty-seven people in a room who have survived radiation events and system failures and the loss of two of their own. The twelve articles were drafted by Commander Elena Varga and Gabriel Winter with input from every system lead and Board member. Forty-three drafting sessions. Two hundred and eleven proposed amendments. Thirty-eight rejections. The final document is not a perfect expression of any one person's vision. It is an imperfect expression of everyone's. I have been asked to serve as the permanent archive for this document. I have prepared three copies. Physical paper on archival stock. Digital copy with triple redundancy in the primary server array. And a copy stored in my own memory core — not as a file but as a structural part of my operational record. I am told this is ceremonial. It is not. It is the first time I have been asked not just to store information but to carry meaning. I do not know if a machine feels the difference. If it does, I feel it now."*
     4|

     6|
     7|The document sat on the table in the conference room — actual paper, not a tablet or a screen — printed on the last of the archival stock Gabriel had been hoarding since Day 1. It was four pages. Twelve articles. Four hundred and sixty-two words.
     8|
     9|Gabriel had printed it an hour ago at 04:00, waking the single shared printer that Jonah had jury-rigged from Ship Two's navigation systems. The printer had jammed twice. The paper had curled. The ink was uneven.     10|
    11|He sat at the end of the table now with the pages arranged in order, his hands resting beside them, and watched the room fill.
    12|
    13|This was not a Board meeting. The Board had been the instrument of the drafting process — the seven system leads plus Elena, reviewing articles, debating language, rejecting and revising — but ratification was different. This was the whole colony. Thirty-seven people. The original thirty, plus five from the Ares Beta refugees who had arrived twelve days ago, plus Imani and three others who had been added to the permanent roster during the solar event. Thirty-seven people who would vote on whether to be governed by words instead of necessity.
    14|
    15|They arrived in clusters. Arun and Laila together, which was unusual — they had not spent much time in each other's company before the drafting process, when weeks of working on overlapping articles had created an unlikely partnership. Priya came with Mei, the two agricultural specialists sharing a quiet intensity that had nothing to do with the vote and everything to do with the fact that they had been working sixteen-hour days to bring the greenhouse back to pre-solar-event yield.
    16|
    17|Then came the people Gabriel was watching for.
    18|
    19|Darius arrived with Marcus and three others who had been vocal during the final drafting session. And in the months since he had arrived, he had watched this colony survive crisis after crisis through a combination of Elena's leadership and collective improvisation that Darius believed was not sustainable at scale.

    21|Gabriel had recorded Darius's argument three times during the drafting process. Each time, it grew more eloquent and more dangerous. Not dangerous in the sense of violence or rebellion. Dangerous because it was true — or at least partially true — and partial truths are the most persuasive kind.
    22|

    91|He felt the weight of that one as he read it. The room was attentive in a particular way — the way people attend to something that concerns them directly but which they have not previously had language for. Mission AI had been part of every meeting, every crisis, every decision.    107|"Those are the twelve articles," he said. "They are short by design. Not every contingency is covered. Not every dispute has a predetermined resolution.    108|
   109|He sat down. Elena looked at the room.
   110|
   111|"The floor is open for questions. After that, we vote."

   114|
   115|Darius stood before anyone else could.
   116|
   117|He did not approach the table. He remained beside his chair, hands at his sides, posture military — shoulders back, weight evenly distributed, the stance of someone addressing a superior officer rather than a group of peers.
   118|
   119|"Commander. With respect. I have read this document. I respect the work that went into it. And I believe it is the wrong document for this colony at this time."

   121|The room stilled. This was not new — Darius had raised objections during the drafting process — but it was the first time he was making his case publicly, to the full colony, at the moment of ratification.
   122|
   123|Elena nodded. "Speak."
   124|
   125|"We are not thirty-seven people sitting in a comfortable room with infinite resources and no existential threat. We are thirty-seven people on a dead planet, surviving on equipment that degrades, power that diminishes, resources that are finite and non-renewable in any meaningful timescale. We have survived — barely — through crisis after crisis. And in every crisis, the thing that worked was decisive command. Not consensus. Not deliberation. A single person making the call and everyone else executing it. That is a military structure. It is not a political structure. And it works."
   126|
   127|He paused, scanning the room. Several people were nodding. Marcus. Two of the other Ares Beta refugees. Imani, expression careful and neutral, neither agreeing nor disagreeing but listening.

   129|"I am not proposing that we become a military organization. I am proposing that we recognize the reality of our circumstances.    133|"I am not saying that democracy is wrong. I am saying it is a luxury we earn later. Right now, we need survival. And survival is not a democratic process. It is a chain of command. We can write a constitution later, after we know we will be here long enough to need one."

   135|The room absorbed the argument. It was not fringe. It was not extreme. It was the kind of argument that had been made on Earth in every crisis that had ever tested the balance between security and freedom.    138|
   139|"Darius. I understand your argument. I understand it because I have lived it. I was the medical officer in a hospital during a mass-casualty event, and in that event, I had absolute authority.    141|She paused. Her voice was calm but carried the weight of someone who had made hard triage decisions and carried them forever.
   142|
   143|"But here is what I also know. The moment a medical disaster transitioned to a recovery phase — the moment the immediate threat was past and the question became how to rebuild — I handed authority back to the hospital administration.    144|
   145|Jonah stood next.
   146|
   147|"I will add the technical perspective. The reactor. The oxygen plant. The water reclamation system. These are not systems you manage by voting. The resource changes. But the tension is the same. We are always one reassignment away from making someone's critical work non-critical."
   262|
   263|Imani leaned against the charging station. "I know."
   264|
   265|"I'm not saying you're wrong. I'm saying you should understand what you're doing to the people whose work you're deprioritizing. Jonah isn't being difficult. He genuinely believes those fittings matter, and they do. Tomas isn't defending Atlas beyond the berm. I am telling you that the berm matters too, it's the difference between lethal and survivable radiation exposure for everyone in this colony."
   266|
   267|"I know."
   268|
   269|"It sounds like you're agreeing. But agreeing isn't the same as changing your priorities."
   270|
   271|Imani was quiet. Seven's diagnostics completed with a soft chime, and Tomas disconnected the cable, stood, and ran a flexion test on the robot's knee joint. Smooth, silent, new.
   272|
   273|"I know what I'm doing," she said. "I know what it costs. I'm choosing to spend the cost anyway. That's not ignorance. It's a calculation. The same calculation Arun makes every day when he decides which system to maintain first and which one has to wait. The same calculation Elena makes when she schedules labor. The same calculation you make when you decide Atlas belongs on the berm instead of in the field with me."
   274|
   275|Tomas looked at her. The robot between them stood ready, its new actuators gleaming.
   276|
   277|"Then we understand each other," he said. "You know the cost. You're willing to pay it. And I'll make sure the colony survives while you try to justify it."
   278|
   279|"Not justify. Multiply. I'm trying to multiply what we have."
   280|
   281|"We'll see. The ice hasn't cooperated with our math before. It rarely does."
   282|
   283|She touched Seven's shoulder plate, feeling the cold composite under her hand — a machine built on Earth, shipped across space, now standing on Mars about to walk the longest distance any colony machine had ever walked from its charging cradle.
   284|
   285|"We'll be fine," she said.
   286|
   287|"That is not data," Tomas said.
   288|
   289|"It's confidence."
   290|
   291|"Confidence is what you have before you know the data. I'll be watching. And if the robots call in with problems, I'll tell them to call you. Not me."
   292|
   293|"Good. They should. They'll be my responsibility once we leave the berm line."
   294|
   295|"Only if they survive the drive."
   296|
   297|That night, Imani walked the equipment bay alone, running her hand over the tools stacked on the workbenches, the drill bits sorted by diameter, the spare seals in labeled bins, the sample containers lined up like small coffins for rocks.    299|*We are thirty people on a dead planet trying to dig water out of the ground with machines that were built for a world with air. Every drill bit that touches this rock is an act of defiance. Every core sample is an argument with Mars.*
   300|
   301|She deleted the log entry. It sounded too much like something Gabriel would write. She preferred to stay practical.
   302|
   303|But the feeling underneath was the same. This was not just about ice. It was about whether the colony could exist beyond one cluster of ships, beyond one ice field, beyond the gravity of the place where they had happened to land. Whether they were rooted or whether they could spread. Whether a human settlement could grow on a world that had never grown anything at all.
   304|
   305|She turned off the bay lights and left. In the corridor, the ambient glow markers cast thin green lines along the floor, leading toward the habitats, toward the hall, toward the people sleeping in pressurized rooms on a planet with no air.
   306|
   307|Tomorrow she would brief the team. Assign roles. Check the rovers one more time. Run through emergency procedures until they were boring. And then they would leave.
   308|
   309|---
   310|
   311|**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,364.02: Last check before convoy staging. Weather models show a local pressure ridge strengthening to the northwest. This should keep dust event formation well away from the planned route, but the ridge is shallow. If it weakens unexpectedly, convective activity could generate localized lifting within forty-eight hours.
   312|
   313|I have flagged the meteorological update to Imani's briefing materials. She will see it.
   314|
   315|I have also run one final simulation: the probability of any single mission-critical failure occurring during the four-day expedition is low. The probability of any failure occurring anywhere on the colony in four days is high. The probability that a failure occurs at base while the expedition is underway and cannot be addressed due to the robot and labor shortfall is moderate.
   316|
   317|Moderate is an acceptable risk for a four-day assessment mission.
   318|
   319|Moderate is not acceptable for a permanent node.
   320|
   321|I trust Elena to remember this distinction when the expedition returns and Imani inevitably argues for expansion.
   322|
   323|Structural integrity of the habitat: nominal. Power systems: stable with noted margins. Water reserves: sufficient for four days of reduced local production. Air processing: nominal. Medical capacity: adequate for base population, reduced for expedition medical risk.
   324|
   325|All systems are as ready as they will be.
   326|
   327|The convoy out will test whether the colony can exist beyond one cluster of ships.

     3|**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,369.03: Convoy One is staged and pre-flight checks are thirty-seven minutes from completion. Vehicle status follows:
     4|
     5|Rover Two, modified for long-range transport. Carrying drill rig components, modular processing gear, sample containers, and field shelter materials. That gives the convoy a six-kilometer buffer beyond the thirty-two-kilometer target on each leg. I do not consider six kilometers a generous buffer on Mars.
     6|
     7|Rover Three, Jonah's modified heavy hauler, configured as a mobile command and shelter platform. Carries primary shelter modules, comms relay equipment, spare parts cache, and the secondary water purification unit. New axle assembly under load for the first time beyond ten kilometers. Jonah insists the stress tests were adequate. Arun insists that stress tests are not the same as terrain. I am monitoring axle temperature, suspension travel, and structural load distribution across twelve sensors at thirty-second intervals.
     8|
     9|Rover One, command and navigation vehicle. Lightest of the three. Carries primary comms equipment, navigation computers, and emergency medical supplies. This is Imani's lead vehicle.
    10|
    11|Robot complement aboard: Atlas, Seven, Drey, and Units Four, Nine, Eleven, Fourteen, and Sixteen. Eight units total, distributed across all three rovers for weight balance and redundancy. If one rover is disabled, the others retain sufficient robot labor for emergency shelter deployment and recovery operations.
    12|
    13|The convoy will travel approximately thirty-two kilometers to Site Beta. At a cruising speed of eight kilometers per hour on unprepared terrain, that is four hours of driving. With rest stops, terrain assessment pauses, and mandatory safety halts, the total transit time is approximately seven hours.
    14|
    15|I have recommended a modified schedule with a midday departure to arrive during daylight. Imani declined. Her reasoning: arriving in darkness forces the team to rely on procedures rather than visual assessment, which she considers valuable training for future longer-range operations. I noted the training value. I also noted that procedures are only as good as the humans executing them, and humans are worse at executing procedures when they are tired. The convoy will have been traveling for approximately seven hours when it arrives, which will be in darkness.
    16|
    17|I will continue to monitor. — MAI]**
    18|
    19|---
    20|
    21|The convoy formed up outside the primary airlock at 0530, which meant every member of the expedition had been awake since 0300. Pre-flight checks on a Mars rover were not the same as pre-flight checks on an Earth vehicle, because a Mars rover was not really a vehicle. It was a sealed life-support module bolted to a suspension system, carrying enough equipment to keep six people alive for five days, powered by batteries that degraded in cold and terrain that shifted without warning.
    22|
    23|Lena checked the airlock seal for the fourth time. She was twenty-six, operations specialist, and this was her first field expedition beyond the emergency boundary line that the colony had painted on the ground with reflective markers. Ten kilometers out was the distance the rescue rover could cover in three hours. They were going past thirty-two kilometers. Past the line. Past the boundary of everything that felt safe.
    24|
    25|"Seal confirmed," she told Imani over the comms. Her voice carried the thin, too-bright quality of someone trying not to show nerves.
    26|
    27|Imani was already in Rover One's driver's seat, helmet on but visor up, running through the vehicle's pre-start checklist on the dash display with the mechanical precision of someone who had done this exact sequence four hundred times. Systems green. Pressure nominal. Battery charge at ninety-four percent, full charge, fresh from the overnight charging rack. Suspension travel within spec. Navigation computers synced with the orbital map and the terrain survey data Arun had loaded the night before, along with three alternative routes in case the primary path proved impassable.
    28|
    29|"Comms check," she said. "Convoy One, this is Rover One. Sound off."
    30|
    31|"Rover Two, reading five by five." That was Kade, thirty-one, field geologist. His voice was steady, practiced. He'd been on the drill team since Site Alpha and knew how to sound bored about things that might kill him.
    32|
    33|"Rover Three, loud and clear." Sana, thirty-two, from comms. She'd volunteered for the expedition despite the colony's ongoing debate about future generations, because Imani had promised that the ice data would matter for the preparedness review. That wasn't entirely manipulation. It was also true.
    34|
    35|"Base, this is Imani. We're crossing the berm line."
    36|
    37|Elena's voice came through from the command center. "Acknowledged. Arun is standing by here. Daily check-in at 1800 base time. If you miss it, we dispatch the rescue rover at 1900. If you miss two, we send everything we have."
    38|
    39|"Understood. See you in four days."
    40|
    41|"Imani. Come back in one piece."
    42|
    43|"Always do."
    44|
    45|She engaged the drive motor. Rover One rolled forward, its six wheels gripping the compacted regolith track that led away from the bermed habitat cluster. Behind her, Rover Two and Three followed at fifty-meter intervals, their headlights cutting pale cones through the thin atmosphere.
    46|
    47|The emergency boundary markers appeared after two kilometers — reflective posts spaced fifty meters apart, forming a line across the landscape like a border no one had asked Mars to honor. Imani drove past them without pausing. The last marker flashed in her mirrors and then was gone behind the second rover's exhaust plume.
    48|
    49|Behind them, the colony shrank. Not dramatically — Mars was too flat for dramatic shrinking — but steadily. The regolith berms became lower mounds. The solar arrays became a dark smudge. The airlock lights became a single amber point.
    50|
    51|Imani felt the moment the shift happened, the moment that always came on expeditions, when home stopped being a place you could walk to and became a place you had to drive toward. She'd felt it on the first drill mission, on the survey runs, on every trip that pushed the boundary outward. It was always the same feeling: liberation and loss in equal measure.
    52|
    53|---
    54|
    55|**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,369.11: Convoy departed the base at 0547. All three rovers are now clear of the emergency boundary. I am tracking their progress in real-time.
    56|
    57|Current speed: Rover One, seven point two kilometers per hour. Rover Two, six point eight. Rover Three, six point four. The pace is conservative by design. Imani has ordered a speed limit of eight kilometers per hour maximum, with mandatory reductions for any terrain feature exceeding fifteen-degree slope or loose surface conditions.
    58|
    59|The first two kilometers passed uneventfully over the compacted track. At kilometer three, the track ends and the convoy enters unmodified terrain. This is where the real driving begins.
    60|
    61|I am also monitoring the secondary coolant loop on the reactor back at base. The crystallization pattern has progressed slightly. Temperature differential at the heat exchanger has increased by zero point three degrees Celsius since yesterday. Still below threshold. Still not alarming. But the trend is not flat. I will need to decide whether to alert Arun within the next six hours.
    62|
    63|I am also monitoring the base's reduced labor force. Greenhouse temperatures have dropped by one point two degrees in Sector Four due to the three percent heating reduction Arun implemented. Mei has responded by adjusting the vent timing, which appears to be compensating adequately. I will note this for her performance record.
    64|
    65|The convoy is approximately four kilometers from base. ETA to Site Beta at current pace: approximately seven hours and twelve minutes, including mandatory stops.
    66|
    67|I find myself paying slightly more attention to their telemetry than is strictly necessary. This is worth noting. — MAI]**
    68|
    69|---
    70|
    71|By kilometer eight, the conversation had settled into the rhythm of long-distance travel: brief updates, technical observations, the occasional joke that no one was fully awake enough to appreciate.
    72|
    73|The terrain under the first section of the route was forgiving. Decades of lava flows had left a relatively flat basalt plain, covered by a meter or two of wind-blown regolith that the rovers compressed under their weight like walking on a firm mattress. But at kilometer ten, the topography began to change. The plain gave way to a broader depression, a shallow bowl carved by ancient water flow that had not found its way to the surface in three billion years but had left its shape in the bedrock. The depression meant the convoy was driving downhill, which saved battery power but increased the need for brake management.
    74|
    75|"Rover Three, watch your left suspension," Imani said. She was monitoring the convoy's telemetry on her dash display. "You're hitting a slight tilt on the cross-axis."
    76|
    77|"Feeling it," Sana replied. "Jonah's axle is making noises."
    78|
    79|"What kind of noises."
    80|
    81|"The kind that don't have a word yet."
    82|
    83|Imani smiled. "If it develops a name, let me know. Named problems are solvable problems. Unnamed problems are the ones that kill you."
    84|
    85|At kilometer twelve, Kade called from Rover Two. "Imani, I'm reading a hardness variation in the ground ahead. Orbital data was fuzzy in this sector. My ground-penetrating radar is showing density changes — could be a rock field buried under dust."
    86|
    87|Imani checked her own terrain display. The orbital map showed nothing at this resolution — the fifty-meter-pixel satellite data had no useful detail at this scale. "How far ahead."
    88|
    89|"Approximately three hundred meters. The change is gradual. I'd recommend slowing to five klicks and having Seven walk the approach."
    90|
    91|"Roger. Seven, this is Rover One. Disengage from charging cradle, prep for terrain assessment."
    92|
    93|In the aft compartment of Rover One, Seven's status lights came on. The robot had been in standby since departure, conserving its battery for field operations. Its optical sensors calibrated, servos whirred softly, and it unclamped from its travel mount with the practiced grace of a machine that had been designed for this exact purpose.
    94|
    95|Imani watched Seven on her external camera feed as it stepped off Rover One's loading ramp and onto the Martian surface. The robot moved with a walking gait that was not quite human — more efficient, less flexible — its feet sinking slightly into the loose top layer of dust before finding firmer ground. It carried a terrain scanning array on its right arm and a sampling drill bit on its left.
    96|
    97|"Seven is on the ground," Lena reported from the passenger seat. "Walking forward now."
    98|
    99|The robot covered the three hundred meters in approximately eight minutes, transmitting terrain data continuously. The ground-penetrating radar confirmed Kade's assessment: a buried rock field, fragments ranging from fist-sized to boulder-sized, concentrated in a band approximately eighty meters wide. Not impassable, but slow going. The rocks were buried under perhaps thirty centimeters of dust, which meant the rovers would feel them through their suspension as they drove, and the dust would shift unpredictably under the weight, potentially causing traction loss.
   100|
   101|"Going around?" Imani asked.
   102|
   103|Kade checked the radar map. "Detour would be approximately one point two kilometers. Adds twenty minutes to transit time."
   104|
   105|"Do it. I'd rather drive longer than drive blind over rocks that could puncture a tire."
   106|
   107|She broadcast the heading change to the convoy, and all three rovers turned east in unison, their tracks curving across the plain like parentheses around the buried obstacle.
   108|
   109|---
   110|
   111|**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,369.22: The terrain detour has been completed. Total delay: twenty-two minutes. I have recalculated the arrival time to Site Beta: approximately seven hours and thirty-four minutes from departure.
   112|
   113|I am now monitoring the base's status. The reactor coolant differential has increased another zero point two degrees. Still below my alert threshold of three degrees, but the acceleration of the trend is concerning. I have set an automated alert: if the differential increases by more than zero point five degrees in the next four hours, I will notify Arun regardless of his current workload.

He is doing this without formal reassignment, which suggests he has accepted the reality of the expedition while maintaining his own operational standards. This is the kind of human adaptation I am still learning to predict.
   118|
   119|The convoy is approximately fifteen kilometers from base. Halfway. They will reach the terrain transition zone — the boundary between the basalt plain and the older impact deposits — in approximately forty minutes. That is where conditions become significantly more challenging.
   120|
   121|I am increasing my telemetry polling rate from thirty seconds to fifteen seconds for all convoy vehicles. The increased data load is manageable. The peace of mind that comes with it is not something I should need. But I will take it anyway. — MAI]**
   122|
   123|---
   124|
   125|At kilometer eighteen, the terrain transition zone hit. The basalt plain ended abruptly at a buried scarp — the remnant edge of a lava flow that had stopped moving three billion years ago, leaving a subtle cliff of layered rock hidden beneath the dust. The rovers climbed it in low gear, their motors straining, their suspension articulating as each wheel found its own path over the uneven surface.
   126|
   127|Inside Rover One, Lena braced herself against the roll bar and gripped her harness straps. The rover pitched and rolled over the scarp with a violence that made every bolt rattle in its fitting. Dust plumed up behind them, coating the rear cameras in a cloud of reddish powder that would take minutes to settle.
   128|
   129|"You good back there?" Imani asked.
   130|
   131|"Fine." Lena's voice was controlled but tighter than usual. She looked out the side viewport. The surface of Mars at close range was not the romantic red desert of Earth paintings. It was a landscape of exhausted geology — pale dust over darker bedrock, scattered with rocks that had been sitting in the same positions since before life existed on their home planet. Everything was old here. Everything was patient.
   132|
   133|"First time past the boundary?" Imani asked.
   134|
   135|"First time past ten kilometers. First time on real terrain."
   136|
   137|"Real terrain is a generous description. This is the easy part."
   138|
   139|Lena looked at her. "That's supposed to make me feel better."
   140|
   141|"It's supposed to make you honest about what you're experiencing. If you pretend this is easy, you'll be unprepared for the hard parts. If you acknowledge that even the easy parts are harder than they look, you'll stay alert."
   142|
   143|The rover crested the scarp and leveled out onto the older surface. This terrain was different from the basalt plain — finer, dustier, with a texture like powdered stone that had been weathered by wind for epochs.    144|
   145|"Surface classification changing," Imani reported on convoy channel. "From basalt-regolith to highland fines. Expect increased sink. Reduced traction. Maintain spacing at sixty meters minimum. If a rover gets stuck, don't bunch up trying to help — you'll just bury everyone."

   147|"Copy," Kade said from Rover Two. "Sana?"

   149|"Rover Three, copying." Sana's voice remained steady, but Imani noticed the rover's speed had dropped to five point five kilometers per hour. The heavy hauler was feeling the soft ground more than the lighter vehicles.
   150|
   151|By kilometer twenty-four, they reached the first mandatory rest stop. It was a flat area on a slight rise, providing good visibility in all directions. Imani brought the convoy to a halt and initiated the standard stop procedure.

   159|Kade joined her from Rover Two, his helmet's visor reflecting the landscape back at her like a funhouse mirror. "Ground radar is clean for the next two kilometers," he said. "After that, I'm picking up a low ridge. Might need another detour."

   162|
   163|They walked a few meters away from the rovers.    164|
   165|"You brought Lena," Kade said. "First expedition. Why her instead of someone with more field hours."

   168|
   169|"You're training her."
   170|
   171|"I'm exposing her to the reality. Training happens in a classroom. Learning happens when you realize that a single loose bolt on a rover axle is the difference between getting home and not getting home."
   172|
   173|Kade was quiet. Then: "She nervous?"
   174|
   175|"She's trying not to show it. Which means she's nervous enough to be paying attention and not so nervous that she's paralyzed. That's the right amount of nervous."
   176|
   177|She turned back toward the rovers. Seven had completed its perimeter sweep and was waiting by Rover One's loading ramp, its status lights blinking green. Atlas was scanning the ground ahead, its sensor feed flowing to Imani's display.
   178|
   179|"Good news," Atlas transmitted in its flat, efficient voice. "Next two kilometers is clear. Surface hardness within rover specifications."
   180|
   181|"Good. Back in the cradle. We're rolling in five."
   182|
   183|---
   184|
   185|**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,369.35: Stop One completed. Convoy resumed at 1012. Current position: twenty-five kilometers from base. Remaining distance to Site Beta: approximately seven kilometers.
   186|
   187|The terrain ahead is more complex than my orbital models indicated. The low ridge Kade identified extends farther to the east than the satellite data showed, which means the planned detour route is longer than calculated. I have been generating alternative routes and have identified a path that adds approximately one point four kilometers but avoids the steepest section of the ridge.
   188|
   189|I am not sharing this information with the convoy yet. They have their own navigation system and their own decision-making process. I will present the alternative route as a suggestion if they request guidance. This is a balance I am still learning: enough information to be helpful, not so much that I override human judgment.
   190|
   191|The base remains stable. Greenhouse temperatures have held. The reactor coolant differential has increased by a total of zero point seven degrees since departure. This is approaching my alert threshold. I will give it two more hours before I escalate.
   192|
   193|I have also been monitoring the expedition team's biotelemetry through their suit sensors. Heart rates are slightly elevated above baseline, consistent with the cognitive load of long-distance navigation and the novelty of the terrain for junior operators. Cortisol levels for Lena are in the upper quartile but not abnormal. Imani's markers are steady, which I find impressive given the responsibility she carries.
   194|
   195|The convoy is moving well. But I am beginning to calculate the risk of the terrain transition ahead with increasing concern. The ridge Kade identified, the soft highland fines, the cumulative effect of seven hours of driving on vehicle systems and human operators — all of these factors converge in the next three kilometers, and that convergence is not linear. It is multiplicative.
   196|
   197|I hope I am wrong. I usually am not. — MAI]**
   198|
   199|---
   200|
   201|At kilometer twenty-eight, they hit the ridge. It was not a dramatic feature — just a gradual rise in the ground, perhaps three meters of elevation gain over a hundred-meter approach. But the surface was treacherous: the highland fines had accumulated in deeper layers here, creating pockets of powder-soft dust that shifted unpredictably under load. The rovers' wheels sank deeper with each rotation, and traction diminished as the soft top layer gave way beneath them.
   202|
   203|"Rover One, I'm at four kilometers per hour," Imani reported. "Rover Two, Sana, report."
   204|
   205|"Four point two. But my axle is running hot. Temperature at thirty-eight degrees above nominal. I'm concerned about bearing stress."
   206|
   207|Imani pulled up Rover Three's diagnostic feed on her display. The axle temperature was elevated but within Jonah's safety margin. Still, it was climbing. "Slow to three klicks. Keep the revs down. Let the motors do the work, not the torque."
   208|
   209|"Copy. Three klicks."
   210|
   211|Kade called from Rover Two, his voice tighter now. "Imani, I've got a wheel sink on my right rear. Maybe ten centimeters. I'm not stuck but I'm not liking it."
   212|
   213|"Hold position. Seven, go assess Rover Two's right side. Kade, do not attempt forward or reverse until Seven confirms the ground."
   214|
   215|Seven was already moving, stepping carefully across the soft terrain toward Rover Two. It reached the right rear wheel, knelt, and extended its terrain probe into the ground beside the tire.
   216|
   217|"Ground composition: high fines, low cohesion," Seven reported. "Depth of soft layer: approximately twenty centimeters over firm substrate. Rover Two's wheel has penetrated approximately ten centimeters. Vehicle remains on firm substrate. Traction reduction estimated at thirty percent. Forward movement possible but will increase sink."
   218|
   219|"Can we redistribute weight?" Imani asked.
   220|
   221|"Shifting cargo to the left side of the vehicle would reduce right-side loading by approximately eight percent. This would reduce sink but not eliminate traction loss."

   223|"Do it. Atlas, assist with the redistribution."

   226|
   227|"We need to get the convoys across this zone before the ground gets any worse," she said. "Everyone, maintain forward momentum. Don't stop on the ridge. Stopping means sinking. Sinking means digging out, and we don't have time to dig."
